Motivation, methods & simulation study

Bayesian SV Clonality Inference

A self-contained Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler — no black-box PPL — motivated by an unresolved measurement artifact in a real 1,493-sample WGS leukemia cohort, validated on three simulated structural-variant cohorts, and worked through end to end: prior specification, posterior sampling, convergence diagnostics, and how purity/ploidy uncertainty propagates into a clonal call.

01

Introduction

Intra-tumor clonal heterogeneity — the coexistence of genetically distinct subclones within a single tumor — is a well-established driver of treatment failure and relapse. A subclone present at diagnosis but below the limit of clinical detection can become the dominant, therapy-resistant population at relapse. Reconstructing the timing of somatic events relative to this clonal architecture — truncal (present in the founding clone, hence in every tumor cell) versus subclonal (acquired later, present in only a fraction) — is therefore not a descriptive exercise but a potential source of prognostic signal: a variant's clonal status at diagnosis is a proxy for how early it arose, and early events are mechanistically more likely to be the drivers that seeded the disease.

Most clonal-reconstruction methods were built around single-nucleotide variants, which are numerous, easy to genotype, and statistically well-behaved. Structural variants (SVs) — deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations — are comparatively underused for this purpose, despite being mechanistically central to B-ALL biology. This is particularly true for RAG-mediated secondary rearrangements: the RAG1/RAG2 recombinase, whose physiological role is V(D)J recombination at the immunoglobulin (IGH/IGL/IGK) and T-cell receptor loci during normal lymphocyte development, is a recognized off-target mutagen in B-cell precursor leukemia — mistargeted RAG activity is implicated in generating secondary structural lesions that cooperate with a founding fusion such as ETV6::RUNX1 to drive leukemogenesis. Whether RAG-locus SVs behave differently in their clonal timing — arising earlier, closer to the founding event, than SVs elsewhere in the genome — is directly testable with this cohort's design, and has a clear line to relapse risk if early RAG-mediated events mark a more aggressive founding clone.

The statistical machinery for asking this well already exists in adjacent form. SNV-focused Bayesian tools (PyClone, DPClust) model cancer cell fraction (CCF) as a latent variable with a proper posterior, and SVclone extends this to structural variants by explicitly correcting for the fact that breakpoint-supporting reads require a minimum soft-clip length to align — a bias reference reads don't share. What most cohort-scale SV pipelines still do in practice, including the current version of this project's pipeline, is simpler: compute CCF as a point-estimate ratio (VAF × ploidy / purity) and cluster it with expectation-maximization. This is fast and interpretable, but it collapses every source of measurement uncertainty — read-count noise, purity/ploidy estimation error, multiplicity ambiguity — into a single number, with no way to express how much to trust it.

That gap is not hypothetical here — it has already produced a concrete, unresolved failure in this project. ETV6::RUNX1, used as a founding-fusion positive control, is expected on basic clonal-evolution grounds to be present in essentially 100% of tumor cells. The current pipeline instead returns a median CCF of 0.55–0.58, with only 15–17% of cases called clonal.

Diagnosed, not yet resolved

Ruled out: double-counting of supporting reads (fixed in an earlier pipeline round); imprecision in the breakpoint detection window (rejected after direct testing). Leading hypothesis: Manta's paired-read-plus-split-read "reference" count does not represent true local sequencing depth for BND (translocation) records the way it does for DEL/DUP/INS — evidenced by non-BND SVs in the same patients, processed by identical purity/ploidy/clustering code, reaching clonal-range CCF. Unconfirmed pending BAM-level verification.

This is exactly the failure mode a point-estimate pipeline cannot self-diagnose: it reports a confidently wrong number rather than a number flagged as unreliable. A Bayesian framework that treats CCF as a posterior distribution — wide when the underlying measurement is untrustworthy, narrow when it isn't — is the natural fix, and is why this is a methodological necessity for this project rather than a stylistic preference.

Aims

  1. Methodological. Develop and validate a Bayesian hierarchical model for SV cancer-cell-fraction estimation that (a) marginalizes multiplicity exactly rather than treating it as a nuisance to be estimated, (b) treats tumor purity as a parameter with an informative prior derived from the CN caller's own uncertainty rather than a plug-in point estimate, and (c) returns posterior credible intervals — not point CCF calls. Validated first on simulated data with known ground truth (complete; §3–7), then applied to the real cohort specifically to diagnose and, where possible, correct the BND-CCF discrepancy.
  2. Biological. Test whether RAG-locus SVs occupy an earlier clonal-timing niche (higher CCF, more often called early-clonal) than off-target or non-RAG SVs, and whether this timing signal — measured with proper uncertainty quantification — is associated with relapse (Relapse_binary).
  3. Validation. Confirm the existing DEL-only positive result (IG-locus > off-target > non-RAG CCF ordering) is preserved under the new Bayesian estimates, and determine whether explicitly modeling BND-specific measurement uncertainty resolves the ETV6::RUNX1 control toward its expected near-clonal status.
02

Methods — the real cohort

2.1 Data source and cohort

Whole-genome tumor-normal pairs from the Genomic Data Commons, SVs called by BRASS (manifest code/gdc_manifest.sv_vcf_1493.txt, 1,493 files). Each VCF (v4.2) reports split-read and spanning-pair support (FORMAT=RC:PS) for tumor and normal samples separately, with sample-level purity (Acf) and ploidy in the ##SAMPLE header. Clinical outcome joins from results/dat_short_include_gap_0921_with_relapse.txt (n=1,485; Relapse_binary: 1,047 non-relapse / 438 relapse).

Not yet addressed

Analyses currently run on the unfiltered raw_structural_variation.vcf.gz calls; PASS- or assembly-score filtering is a planned refinement, not yet applied.

2.2 Baseline pipeline (current, point-estimate)

VAF = tumor_support / (tumor_support + normal_support) from RC:PS — BRASS does not report true reference-read depth, so this is a support-ratio proxy for VAF, not a direct allele fraction, an existing documented limitation. CCF = VAF × ploidy / purity; the current pipeline (svclonality/run_cohort_ccf.py, ccflib.py) applies per-locus copy-number correction and cohort-wide EM clustering, superseding an earlier per-patient GMM version. Clonal timing: early-clonal (CCF ≥ 0.8), subclonal-major (0.4–0.8), subclonal-minor (< 0.4). RAG-locus timing is computed separately in svclonality/rag_clonal_timing.py. Driver SVs intersect the BRASS GENE field with the COSMIC Cancer Gene Census (recurrence ≥ 5 patients). Group comparisons use the Mann-Whitney U test.

2.3 Diagnosing the BND artifact

Within the same patients, CCF was compared for BND versus non-BND records under identical purity, ploidy, and clustering code. Non-BND SVs reach clonal-range CCF in these patients; BND SVs — including ETV6::RUNX1 itself — do not. Two alternative explanations (double-counted supporting reads; an imprecise breakpoint window inflating apparent reference support) were tested and rejected. The leading hypothesis — that Manta's combined paired+split-read "reference" count systematically understates true local depth specifically for BND records — remains unconfirmed pending BAM-level access.

2.4 Proposed Bayesian extension

Extending the model formalized in §3 from simulation to real application:

  • Purity as a parameter, not a plug-in. ρ's prior centers on the VCF-header Acf value, with prior width set from the CN caller's own confidence — rather than substituting Acf directly into the CCF formula as done currently.
  • SV-class-specific overdispersion. Fit the beta-binomial overdispersion s separately for BND versus DEL/DUP/INV/INS records. If the Manta ref-count hypothesis is correct, BND records should require a much lower (noisier) s to fit — a falsifiable, purely statistical test that doesn't require BAM access. Calibration source for s (repeated breakpoint calls, or high-confidence non-BND SVs with independently known clonal status) still needs to be finalized — there's no germline-het-SNP baseline available in an SV-only pipeline the way there is for SNVs.
  • Sampler. The Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler validated in §4, fit per patient initially; a cohort-level hierarchical extension (partial pooling of overdispersion and purity priors across patients) is natural future work, not part of the initial implementation.
  • Output. Posterior CCF credible intervals per SV and posterior P(clonal), with high-uncertainty records (e.g. BND) explicitly flagged rather than silently assigned a point value.

2.5 Validation plan

CheckStatusCriterion
Sampler convergence & purity propagation on simulated dataComplete split-R̂ < 1.02, ESS in the hundreds–thousands; see §5–7
Internal consistencyPending DEL-only IG-locus > off-target > non-RAG CCF ordering preserved under new posterior estimates
Biological positive controlPending ETV6::RUNX1 posterior CCF shifts materially toward clonal (e.g. posterior mean > 0.9) once BND-specific overdispersion is modeled

The success criterion for the BND fix is pre-specified: a large, quantified shift in ETV6::RUNX1 posterior CCF away from 0.55–0.58, not a vague expectation that the number improves.

2.6 Downstream: relapse association under uncertainty

Once per-SV CCF posteriors are available, the RAG-locus-vs-relapse association (Aim 2) is tested by propagating posterior uncertainty into the group comparison — drawing from the CCF posterior (analogous to the multiple-imputation approach used for purity uncertainty in §6) rather than testing a single point-estimate clonal/subclonal label — before applying the existing Mann-Whitney / logistic-regression framework already used for the Relapse_binary comparison.

03

Generative model, likelihood & priors

The general model referenced in §2.4, derived here from first principles — not just stated — since every step exists to answer a specific "why."

3.1 Notation

SymbolMeaning
i = 1..Nindex over SVs
k = 1..Kindex over clusters (truncation level of the mixture)
ai, dialt read count and total depth at SV i (ref count = di−ai)
CNitotal copy number at the SV locus in tumor cells (input from a CN caller)
ρtumor purity (aberrant cell fraction)
φkcancer cell fraction of cluster k
zi ∈ {1..K}cluster assignment of SV i
π = (π1,…,πK)mixture weights
mi ∈ {1..CNi}multiplicity: copies of the variant allele among CNi total copies
sbeta-binomial concentration (inverse-overdispersion)

3.2 Deriving the VAF equation from an allele-counting argument

A tumor sample is a mixture of normal cells (fraction 1−ρ) and tumor cells (fraction ρ). Within the tumor compartment, a sub-fraction φk carries a given SV. At that locus, a variant-carrying tumor cell holds m copies of the variant allele out of CNi total copies; a non-carrying tumor cell holds 0 variant copies out of the same CNi; a normal cell holds 0 variant copies out of 2 (diploid). The expected VAF is the ratio of two population averages — expected variant allele copies per cell, over expected total allele copies per cell:

E[variant copies / cell]  =  ρ·φk·m  +  ρ(1−φk)·0  +  (1−ρ)·0  =  ρ·φk·m
E[total copies / cell]  =  ρ·CNi  +  (1−ρ)·2
E[ VAFi ]  =  ρ · φk · m ρ · CNi + 2(1−ρ)
the same "weighted-average allele count" argument used in ASCAT / Battenberg / PyClone; nothing SV-specific yet
Why derive it instead of stating it

Writing it as a ratio of two expectations — not just pattern-matching the formula — is what lets you answer follow-ups by re-deriving instead of recalling: e.g. "what if the normal cells aren't diploid at this locus" just changes the "2" to CNnormal in the denominator, which falls straight out of the same argument.

3.3 From expected VAF to a read-count likelihood

Read counts are noisy realizations of the expected VAF, and naively one reaches for ai | di ~ Binomial(di, VAF). Real SV read counts are more variable than that: mapping bias, local coverage fluctuation, and PCR duplication all inflate the variance beyond what a fixed-p binomial predicts. The standard fix treats the per-read success probability itself as random rather than fixed, centered on the expected VAF with a concentration parameter s controlling how tightly:

pi  ~  Beta( VAFi·s, (1−VAFi)·s )
ai | di, pi  ~  Binomial(di, pi)
⇩  marginalize pi analytically (Beta-Binomial compound distribution)
ai | di  ~  BetaBinomial(di, VAFi·s, (1−VAFi)·s)
P(ai|di,α,β) = C(di,ai) · B(ai+α, di−ai+β) / B(α,β),   α=VAF·s, β=(1−VAF)·s
Why this specific fix, and what s means

s is literally an inverse-overdispersion knob: as s→∞, Var(pi)→0 and the model collapses back to plain Binomial(di, VAF) — so beta-binomial strictly generalizes binomial rather than replacing it, and s can be read as an effective "prior sample size" behind the read-level rate. This is why s is a natural target for empirical calibration (from germline het SNPs, or from repeated breakpoint calls — §9) rather than a free tuning knob.

3.4 Multiplicity: a discrete nuisance parameter, marginalized exactly

mi ∈ {1,…,CNi} is unknown per SV. Rather than sample it, place a discrete uniform prior and sum it out of the likelihood before it ever reaches the sampler:

P(ai | di, CNi, ρ, φzi, s)  =  (1/CNi) · ∑m=1…CNi BetaBinom( ai; di, VAF(m)·s, (1−VAF(m))·s )
Why marginalize rather than sample m

Two independent reasons. (1) It's exact, not an approximation — for any discrete latent variable with small enumerable support, summing it out of the likelihood is precisely equivalent to sampling it and averaging, in the limit of infinite samples, but costs one sum instead of an entire extra MCMC dimension. (2) Rao-Blackwellization — collapsing (marginalizing) a variable out of a Monte Carlo estimator can only reduce estimator variance, by the Rao-Blackwell theorem; this is textbook "collapsed Gibbs sampling," and naming it signals the marginalization was a deliberate variance-reduction choice, not a shortcut.

3.5 Cluster structure: why a Bayesian nonparametric motivation, and the finite compromise actually used

The real object of inference is a partition of N SVs into an unknown number of clusters. Fixing K in advance forces an awkward outer model-selection loop (fit at several K, compare by BIC/WAIC). The Bayesian-nonparametric answer is a Dirichlet Process mixture, most concretely via its stick-breaking construction:

G  ~  DP(α, G0)     (stick-breaking form)
βk  ~  Beta(1, α),    k = 1, 2, …     πk  =  βk ∏j<k(1−βj)
K is inferred from data, not fixed — the "right" model in the sense that it doesn't force a discrete model-selection decision

What's actually implemented is a sparse finite mixture — K=6 truncation, π ~ Dirichlet(α/K, …, α/K). As K→∞ with α/K held so the total concentration stays fixed, this finite-dimensional Dirichlet converges to the DP (the Ishwaran & James 2001 finite-approximation result); using a small per-component concentration α/K < 1 induces the same "rich get richer" sparsity the DP exhibits — the posterior naturally empties out unused components rather than spreading mass evenly — without stick-breaking machinery or infinite-dimensional data augmentation.

Why symmetric Dirichlet specifically

A symmetric Dirichlet(α/K,…) prior on π is exchangeable across the K labels — no built-in preference for which integer index is "cluster 1." That's not incidental: labels genuinely are arbitrary, label-switching is an expected symmetry of any mixture posterior, and this is precisely why convergence diagnostics later (§5) must be computed only on label-invariant functionals.

3.6 The clonal anchor, formalized as an identifiability argument

Fixing φ1 := 1 (not sampled) isn't a convenience — it's the fix for a real non-identifiability. For a single SV with CN=2, m=1, VAF ≈ ρφ/2: to leading order the likelihood is a function of the product ρφ only,

L(ρ, φ)  ≈  f(ρ·φ)
level sets of L are curves ρ·φ = const — a 1-D ridge in a 2-D parameter space; formally, the Fisher information matrix for (ρ,φ) from a single SV is rank-deficient along the direction orthogonal to ∇(ρφ)

ρ and φ are therefore not jointly identified by any single SV's data. Fixing φ1=1 collapses that ridge to a single point for cluster-1 members, which then pins ρ from those SVs' data alone; every other cluster's φk is then identified relative to that shared, now-pinned ρ. This is the load-bearing design choice in the whole model — see §4.6 for how it also explains why mean-field VI is the wrong tool here.

ParameterPriorRationale
πDirichlet(α/K, …, α/K), K = 6 truncation Sparse finite mixture, §3.5 — a cheap stand-in for a DP prior that lets K adapt without full nonparametric machinery.
φ1fixed at 1.0 Clonal anchor, §3.6 — resolves the ρ·φ identifiability ridge.
φ2..KUniform(0,1)Flat — no prior preference for subclone size.
ziCategorical(π)Cluster membership.
miUniform over {1,…,CNi} Not sampled — marginalized exactly, §3.4.
ρBeta(aρ,bρ) matched to (mean, sd) from a CN caller Informative, not a plug-in point estimate — §6–7 treat this prior's width as an experimental variable.
Design choice

Sparse finite mixture vs. a true Dirichlet process (stick-breaking, Neal 2000 Algorithm 8): the DP is more principled and is the "right" answer in the abstract, but it forces MCMC — no closed-form CAVI/mean-field update exists for a non-conjugate base measure over a beta-binomial likelihood. The finite sparse mixture (this report, and the approach behind PyClone-VI — benchmarked directly in §8) gets a workable stand-in that could, in principle, also be fit by VI.

04

Posterior derivation & sampling

4.1 The joint posterior — the "master equation"

Every sampler step below is derived by isolating the terms that involve one variable from this single joint density and renormalizing. Writing it out once, in full, up front:

p(ρ, π, φ, z | a, d, CN)  ∝
∏i BetaBinomm(ai | di, CNi, ρ, φzi, s)  [likelihood, m marginalized]
× ∏i πzi  [zi | π]
× Dirichlet(π; α/K,…,α/K)  [π prior]
× ∏k=2K Uniform(φk; 0,1)  [φ prior, φ1≡1]
× Beta(ρ; aρ, bρ)  [ρ prior]

4.2 zi | rest — exact categorical Gibbs

Isolating the terms containing zi from §4.1:

p(zi=k | rest)  ∝  πk · BetaBinomm(ai | di, CNi, ρ, φk, s)
a finite (K-way) discrete distribution — normalize by summing over k=1..K, then sample directly
Why exact

Conditional on π, ρ, φ, the zi's are independent across i and each has a finite discrete support — no approximation, no tuning, no acceptance/rejection needed.

4.3 π | z — exact conjugate Gibbs

p(π | z)  ∝  Dirichlet(π; α/K,…,α/K) · ∏k πknk,    nk = #{i : zi=k}
          =  Dirichlet(π; α/K+n1, …, α/K+nK)
Dirichlet is conjugate to the categorical/multinomial likelihood — standard result, exact update

4.4 φk | rest, k = 2…K — Metropolis-Hastings on the logit scale

Isolating φk's terms leaves a flat prior times a beta-binomial likelihood restricted to cluster k's current members — no standard conjugate family absorbs a beta-binomial pmf as a function of its own shape parameter, so this step needs Metropolis-Hastings.

Why the logit transform specifically

φk ∈ (0,1). A Gaussian random-walk proposal directly on φk either wastes draws proposing out-of-support values, or needs a bounded/truncated proposal whose asymmetry complicates the Hastings ratio. Working on xk = logit(φk) = log(φk/(1−φk)) ∈ ℝ makes a plain symmetric Gaussian random walk valid, at the cost of a Jacobian correction since the density I actually want draws from is in φ-space: |∂φk/∂xk| = φk(1−φk).

xk'  =  logit(φk) + ε,    ε ~ N(0, step²)   →   φk' = logit&supminus;¹(xk')
αMH  =  min { 1,  Lk(φk') · φk'(1−φk') Lk(φk) · φk(1−φk)  }
Lk = product of BetaBinomm over SVs currently assigned to cluster k; the flat Uniform(0,1) prior contributes a constant that cancels

4.5 ρ | rest — Metropolis-Hastings, likelihood pooled over all SVs

Same non-conjugacy issue, but now every SV's VAF depends on ρ (not just one cluster's members), so the likelihood term is a product over all i, and the prior is no longer flat — Beta(aρ,bρ) contributes a real ratio, not a cancelling constant:

αMH  =  min { 1,  L(ρ') · Beta(ρ'; aρ,bρ) · ρ'(1−ρ') L(ρ) · Beta(ρ; aρ,bρ) · ρ(1−ρ)  }
L(ρ) = ∏i BetaBinomm(ai | di, CNi, ρ, φzi, s) — every SV contributes, regardless of cluster

4.6 Why MCMC over VI, formalized

A mean-field VI fit would posit q(ρ,π,φ,z) = q(ρ)·q(π)·q(φ)·q(z) — i.e. it assumes posterior independence between ρ and φ. But §3.6 just showed the true posterior has exactly the opposite structure: ρ and any φk are coupled through the same likelihood via their product, a correlation mean-field cannot represent by construction. Mean-field typically still recovers reasonable marginal means (which is why VI point estimates are often fine) but systematically understates marginal variances — precisely because it can't let uncertainty in one direction be partially explained by the other. That is the specific failure mode this report is built to characterize (§6–7), which is why the core results use MCMC, with VI reserved for a fast initial screen cross-checked against MCMC on a subset — and it's exactly what shows up empirically in the PyClone-VI benchmark in §8.

4.7 Uncertainty propagation, formalized

The correctly-marginalized posterior CCF for SV i integrates out the uncertain purity:

p(φzi | data)  =  ∫ p(φzi | data, ρ) · p(ρ | data) · dρ
Why joint sampling is sufficient — no extra integration step

Because ρ is sampled jointly with φ and z at every iteration, each post-burn-in draw of φzi already reflects one particular ρ drawn from its own posterior — so simply collecting φzi across iterations gives Monte Carlo draws from exactly the integral above, automatically. A plug-in approach that fixes ρ=ρ̂ and computes p(φzi | data, ρ̂) is the degenerate special case of this same integral using a point mass p(ρ|data)=δ(ρ−ρ̂) instead of the true posterior — provably discarding all purity-driven variance, not just approximating it away.

MCMC vs. VI, short version

A mean-field VI fit would be far cheaper here, but ρ and φ enter the likelihood as a product — they are structurally correlated in the posterior — and mean-field explicitly assumes independence across factors. That's precisely where VI would understate the joint uncertainty this report is trying to characterize (§4.6–4.7), which is why the MCMC version is the primary result, with VI as a fast initial screen cross-checked against MCMC on a subset.

Experiment 1 — does it converge?

120 simulated SVs, purity 0.65, three true clones (CCF 1.00 / 0.55 / 0.22, weights 0.40 / 0.35 / 0.25), 20% of loci on a copy-gained segment (CN = 3) to add realistic multiplicity ambiguity.

R̂ and ESS above are computed only on label-invariant quantities — log-likelihood, ρ, occupied cluster count, and per-SV assigned CCF — never on a raw φk trace by cluster index, which is meaningless once labels can permute between chains.

Reading it honestly: the CCF=0.22 clone (bottom-right block) separates cleanly. The CCF=1.00 and CCF=0.55 clones blend into each other more than I'd like — their VAFs (0.325 vs. 0.179 at ρ=0.65) are far enough apart in principle, but the copy-gain multiplicity ambiguity and beta-binomial noise erode some of that gap in practice. The model still recovers three-to-four effective clusters (posterior mode 4 against a K=6 truncation and 3 true clusters — the extra cluster is the sparse prior's normal tendency to keep a small satellite occupied), which is the expected, defensible behavior, not a failure.

06

Experiment 2 — purity uncertainty propagation

Same well-separated 3-clone cohort, refit under four purity priors, to see how much of the CN caller's own uncertainty survives into the CCF posterior and into a clonal/subclonal call at threshold 0.85.

ScenarioPrior meanPrior sdPosterior ρMean post. sd(φ)Calls flipped vs. A
A · correct, confident0.650.030.6430.116—
B · correct, uncertain0.650.120.6670.1410
C · underestimated0.550.030.5510.1320
D · overestimated0.750.030.7500.0980
Finding

Posterior spread in CCF widens monotonically with the purity prior's own width (0.116 → 0.141 as sd goes 0.03 → 0.12) — uncertainty does propagate — but for this clonal structure, even a confidently-wrong purity prior (±0.10, scenario C/D) never flips a threshold call, because the clones sit far enough apart (CCF 1.00 / 0.55 / 0.22) that a purity shift moves everyone's estimate together without crossing 0.85. That robustness is conditional on separation, not general — see §7.

07

Experiment 3 — a deliberately hard case

Experiment 2's clones are far apart, so it under-sells how purity bias actually breaks clonality calls in practice. This one is built specifically to fail: 200 SVs, two clones at CCF 1.00 and 0.75 — close enough to straddle a 0.85 clonal-call threshold — CN=2 throughout, depth ~100×.

Unplanned finding, kept in

A pilot check (evaluating the likelihood at the true ρ and φ, no sampling at all) found single-SV MAP classification accuracy of only ~75–80% under comparable depth/noise settings — even with the correct parameters handed to the model. A CCF gap of 0.25 at ~100× WGS depth is simply close to the per-read noise floor set by the beta-binomial overdispersion; more MCMC iterations cannot fix an identifiability limit set by the data itself. This is the reason real pipelines (PyClone, DPClust, SVclone) pool hundreds of mutations per cluster rather than trusting any single variant's own classification.

Two things are true in Fig. 5 at once, and both are worth having ready:

  • The direction and magnitude match theory. Underestimating ρ inflates the CCF estimate needed to explain a fixed VAF (denominator effect in the equation in §3); overestimating ρ deflates it. The curve is monotonic and roughly linear — about a 0.03–0.05 CCF shift per 0.04 purity-prior shift — which is exactly the propagation mechanism the question is testing for.
  • The baseline (bias = 0) sits at 0.55, not the true 0.75. This is a hard-clustering selection effect, not a purity artifact: when two components overlap this much, the SVs a Gibbs sweep assigns to the "subclone" cluster are enriched for the low-VAF tail of both populations (the low outliers of the true clonal cluster, plus the low half of the true subclone), which pulls that cluster's mean down — a truncation/selection bias familiar from mixture-model literature, distinct from (and stacking with) the purity effect.

Net: this configuration never actually crosses the 0.85 threshold, so it doesn't produce a clean flip — but a cohort where the true subclone sits at 0.80–0.83 instead of 0.75 plausibly would, given the same ~0.03–0.05-per-shift dose-response. I'd rather bring the honest, more interesting result (a real selection-bias mechanism, correctly diagnosed) than a cleaner number I hadn't actually earned.

08

Benchmark against existing methods

"How does this compare to what already exists" is the natural next question after any new method, so this section runs it. Three methods were actually installed and fit to the identical simulated cohort used in Experiment 1 (n=120 SVs, purity 0.65, true clones CCF 1.00/0.55/0.22); two more (SVclone, SVCFit) are compared at the methodology/reported-performance level because standing them up live was not tractable within the scope of this write-up — both are reported honestly below, including why.

8.2 Diagnosing the gap, honestly — including a hypothesis that didn't survive testing

PyClone-VI beats this report's model on both RMSE and ARI on this particular simulated instance. Rather than pick a comfortable explanation, I tested the obvious one directly.

Hypothesis 1, tested and rejected

"My model is worse because it's honestly carrying ρ uncertainty that PyClone-VI is simply handed as truth." To test this I reran the sampler with ρ's prior collapsed to sd=0.005 — effectively fixed, matching PyClone-VI's information exactly. Result: RMSE 0.338→0.338, ARI 0.221→0.221, unchanged to four decimal places. Purity uncertainty is not the explanation. Good news for the report's central claim (§6–7 don't hinge on this), bad news for this particular excuse.

The more likely explanation, consistent with evidence already in this report rather than a new assumption:

  • Experiment 1 already showed this exact weakness, on this exact dataset. Fig. 3's posterior similarity matrix shows the CCF=1.00 and CCF=0.55 clusters partially blending — a genuine, previously-documented identifiability limit, not something new introduced by this benchmark. A worse ARI here is the expected downstream consequence of a fact already on the record.
  • Mean-field VI is known to produce overconfident (lower-entropy) posteriors — the same structural property derived formally in §4.6, there in the context of ρ-φ correlation, here showing up as a different symptom: a crisper, more decisive point partition. My sampler pools four honest MCMC chains via a Binder-loss-consistent posterior-similarity-matrix procedure (§5), which correctly blends together SVs the posterior is genuinely unsure about — that's the right Bayesian behavior when the boundary is ambiguous, but it costs ARI against a single ground-truth partition precisely when the truth happens to sit inside that ambiguous region.
  • PyClone-VI's optimization framing helps it here. 10 VI restarts, keep the best by ELBO, is a multistart optimization procedure aimed at the single best local solution. Pooling 4 MCMC chains is not optimization — it's an honest average over the full posterior, including any chain whose stochastic path spent more time in a less-clean partition. Those are different objects to report, and the "best of 10" one will often look better on a single ground-truth comparison even when it is not more correct about the actual uncertainty.
Falsifiable follow-up I'd want to run next

PyClone-VI reports a per-SV cluster_assignment_prob; my sampler's posterior similarity matrix gives an equivalent per-SV assignment confidence. Directly comparing the two distributions — is PyClone-VI's confidence systematically higher for the same ambiguous SVs my model is honestly unsure about — would either confirm or kill the mean-field-overconfidence explanation quantitatively rather than by inference. I'd want that comparison in hand before repeating this explanation to a room that works on VI for a living.

8.3 SVclone and SVCFit — not run live, and why

Both are real, actively cited tools for exactly this problem; both were evaluated for feasibility and neither was completed live, for the concrete, checkable reasons below.

ToolStatus this sessionWhy not completedWhat it does (from paper/README, not re-verified here)
SVclone
(Cmero et al. 2020, Nat Commun)		 Bioconda dependency solve succeeded (svclone=1.1.4 + r-ccube, R 4.4) after two failed attempts to find a compatible R/ccube build pin; the download step then hit a cluster-wide login-node thread/network contention issue (same root cause documented in §7's infra note) that interrupted the run before install completed. Re-attempt via sbatch once the transient contention clears — the solve is already known to work, so this is very likely a 10-minute job, not a dead end. 5-stage pipeline (annotate/count/filter/cluster/post-assign); R/ccube Dirichlet-process mixture clustering; explicit VAF bias correction for breakpoint-supporting reads' minimum soft-clip requirement — the SV-specific correction this report's model does not have (§9).
SVCFit
(Karchin Lab, bioRxiv 2025)		 Not attempted. Depends on a full external tool chain (GATK4, Manta, SVtyper, FACETS, bcftools, samtools) to produce its required input files — standing that up is a multi-day systems task, out of scope for this write-up. Models SV-type-specific breakpoint/breakend read patterns plus local copy-number context; notably does not require a purity point estimate as input — a different design philosophy from this report's informative-prior approach. Claims lower error than SVclone on simulated single- and multi-clone benchmarks in its preprint (self-reported, not independently re-verified here).
09

What's simplified here, and how I'd extend it

  • Overdispersion s is fixed, not given a hyperprior calibrated from germline heterozygous SNP allele counts in the same BAM — the standard way to get a data-driven value.
  • Sparse finite mixture, not a true DP — Neal (2000) Algorithm 8 for a non-conjugate base measure is the principled version; I'd reach for it once the finite approximation's sensitivity to K is checked.
  • Classic split-R̂, not rank-normalized (Vehtari et al. 2021) — the modern diagnostic is more robust to heavy-tailed posteriors and is what I'd actually report.
  • No SNV+SV joint clustering. SNVs are far more numerous and individually better identified; anchoring the clonal tree on SNVs first and placing SVs onto the resulting clusters (the SVclone strategy) would sidestep exactly the per-SV weak-identifiability problem Experiment 3 surfaces.
  • No SV-specific VAF bias correction. Breakpoint-supporting reads need a minimum soft-clip to align, which reference reads don't — SVclone corrects for this using the read length and insert-size distribution; omitting it here means the simulated VAFs are cleaner than real SV data.
  • No diagnosis–relapse joint model. The real scientific question is relapse risk; a longitudinal two-timepoint clustering that tracks CCF change per clone is the natural next step, not single-timepoint clonality in isolation.
  • No orthogonal validation. Nanopore long reads can directly count molecules spanning a breakpoint — a validation layer this simulation, by construction, doesn't need but real data does.

Reproducibility: bayesian_sv_clonality.py, fixed seeds per scenario, run under conda env torch-env on the USC CARC debug partition.
